title: You Stopped Placing Amalgam. Your Patients Still Have Them.
html:
Ask most general dentists when they last placed an amalgam restoration, and many will need a moment to remember. Ask when they last removed one, and the answer is probably this week.

That gap sits at the center of a compliance issue many practices assume no longer applies to them: Amalgam placement in the United States has fallen sharply, but amalgam removal has not. Under federal rules, removing amalgam carries the same wastewater obligations as placing it.

Placement is Down, but the Installed Base is Not.

The decline in new amalgam restorations is well documented. A JADA study of electronic health records found that the amalgam restoration rate in FDA-identified at-risk populations fell from 21.8% in 2017 to 4.1% in 2023.1 Globally, parties to the Minamata Convention on Mercury agreed in November 2025 to phase out dental amalgam by 2034.2

Decades of earlier placement, however, remain in patients’ mouths. By one estimate, 100 million people in the United States have amalgam fillings.3 Using national survey data, the ADA Science & Research Institute found that 51.5% of restored teeth in the U.S. population contained amalgam in 2015–2016. Among people with restored teeth, the average number of amalgam-restored teeth rose with age, from 4.71 in 15–24-year-olds to 7.03 in adults 75 and older.4 A separate analysis of 2015–2018 data confirmed that amalgam restorations are more common in older adults, while non-amalgam materials now dominate in adults under 40.5

The patients on today’s schedule carry a large inventory of aging amalgam. When those restorations fracture, develop recurrent decay, or are replaced for other clinical reasons, they are drilled out, and the particles go straight into the practice’s vacuum system.

Why Removal Triggers Compliance

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) identifies dental offices as the main source of mercury discharges to publicly owned treatment works (POTWs) and estimates that about 103,000 U.S. offices use or remove amalgam. Mercury enters wastewater both when new fillings are placed and when old ones are drilled out. At the treatment plant, much of it settles into sewage sludge, which can carry it into the environment through incineration, landfilling, or land application. Mercury is a potent neurotoxin that bioaccumulates in fish and shellfish.6

The EPA Dental Effluent Guidelines (40 CFR Part 441) apply to practices that place or remove amalgam. The exemption for non-placing offices is narrow: it covers practices that do not place amalgam and do not remove it except in limited emergency or unplanned, unanticipated circumstances, and those practices must certify that status to their Control Authority.7 A general practice that routinely replaces old amalgams does not qualify. Local Control Authorities can set requirements stricter than the federal rule, so practices should confirm what their own Control Authority requires. The EPA expects the rule to cut mercury discharges to POTWs by 5.1 tons per year.6

The Four Components of Compliance

1. Amalgam Separator

The Rule requires a separator certified to ISO 11143 or ANSI/ADA Specification 108 with at least 95% removal efficiency, sized for the practice’s maximum wastewater flow. It must be inspected according to the manufacturer’s operating manual, and its collection container replaced on the manufacturer’s schedule or when it reaches the maximum fill level, whichever comes first. A malfunctioning unit must be repaired or replaced within 10 business days.7 The Solmetex® NXT Hg5® Amalgam Separator is ISO 11143 certified with a capture rate of 99.9% and installs inline with the existing vacuum system. When its collection container is full, the practice swaps it out and sends it for recycling. Because it is integrated into the vacuum system, the separator works in the background on every procedure, providing always-on compliance with no extra steps for the clinical team.

One date deserves attention now: Any amalgam separator installed before June 14, 2017, satisfy the certification and sizing requirements only until they are replaced or until June 14, 2027, whichever comes first.7 Practices running older units should confirm their equipment meets current requirements before that deadline. This is a one-time replacement date.

2. Neutral-pH Vacuum Line Cleaner

Waterlines, chairside traps, and evacuation lines that discharge amalgam wastewater must not be cleaned with oxidizing or acidic cleaners, including bleach, chlorine, iodine, and peroxide, with a pH below 6 or above 8.7Cleaners outside that range can redissolve captured mercury and release it back into the wastewater stream, defeating the purpose of the separator. A neutral-pH vacuum line cleaner, used daily and after procedures with heavy blood or debris, keeps captured mercury where it belongs while removing accumulated buildup in vacuum lines that may affect suction performance. Solmetex® PowerScrub® is a non-foaming, neutral-pH vacuum line cleaner made for this purpose.

3. Amalgam Waste Collection

The separator handles amalgam in the vacuum stream, but the rule also prohibits discharging waste amalgam from chairside traps, screens, vacuum pump filters, dental tools, cuspidors, and collection devices.7 This material, along with extracted teeth containing amalgam and any spent amalgam capsules, belongs in a dedicated amalgam waste container sent for recycling rather than in regular trash or down the drain. The Solmetex® Practice Waste Solutions Amalgam Bucket serves this role and is recycled annually or when full, whichever occurs first.

4. Documentation

Compliance has to be demonstrable. Every practice subject to the rule must file a One-Time Compliance Report with its Control Authority and keep it on file for as long as the practice operates. A new owner must file a new report within 90 days of a transfer. For at least three years, in paper or electronic form, the practice must also keep:7

  • Date, person, and results of each separator inspection, plus any follow-up actions
  • Documentation of collection container replacement
  • Dates amalgam waste was picked up or shipped for disposal, and the name of the receiving facility
  • Any separator repair or replacement, including make and model
  • The manufacturer’s operating manual for the current unit

An online portal such as Solmetex’s My Solutions Center keeps recycling certificates for collection containers and waste buckets accessible 24/7, so records are easy to produce when an inspector asks.

The Bottom Line: Amalgam Removal Will Outlast Placement

Choosing not to place amalgam is a clinical decision. It does not change the compliance obligations of a practice that removes it. With an estimated 100 million Americans carrying amalgam fillings, and amalgam most concentrated in older patients, removal will continue long after placement ends. A certified separator, a neutral-pH line cleaner, dedicated waste collection, and current records protect local waterways and keep the practice inspection-ready. Once the system is in place, maintaining it takes minimal effort.
